summary: Defines the vCard data format for representing and exchanging information about people and other entities, such as names, addresses, email, phone numbers, photos, and logos. It replaced RFCs 2425, 2426, and 4770 and updated RFC 2739.

plainLanguage.summary: vCard is a text format for contact details, such as a person's name, phone number, and address. RFC 6350 defines a shared version so different address-book programs can exchange those details.

questions: how do vcard lines get folded
subtitle: A text format for exchanging contact details between different address books.

tldr.problem: Address books run on many devices and platforms, so they need a shared format for capturing and exchanging contact information.
tldr.mechanism: A vCard 4.0 is UTF-8 text made of named property lines inside BEGIN:VCARD and END:VCARD markers. Parameters describe a property's value or role, and synchronization identifiers help match cards and properties.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6350 defines vCard 4.0, obsoletes RFCs 2425, 2426, and 4770, and updates RFC 2739. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6868, RFC 9554, and RFC 9555.

today: RFC 6350 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2425, RFC 2426, and RFC 4770, updates RFC 2739, and has itself been updated by RFC 6868, RFC 9554, and RFC 9555.

sections.title: A Shared Format for Contact Data
sections.content:
RFC 6350 defines vCard, a format for capturing and exchanging information normally kept in an address book or directory. A vCard can describe an individual or another entity and can carry names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, photographs, and other information.

The document specifies the text/vcard content type and version 4.0 of the format. It is intended to work across the different platforms that exchange contact data.

The RFC uses requirement words such as MUST and SHOULD with their standard meanings. Its rules describe how a valid card is structured and how programs should handle its properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Address books store contact details in many places and formats. vCard gives programs a shared text format for exchanging those details.

sections.title: The Structure of a vCard
sections.content:
A vCard uses UTF-8 and lines separated by CRLF. A card begins with BEGIN:VCARD, has VERSION:4.0 immediately after it, and ends with END:VCARD. Each card MUST include the FN property, which gives its formatted name.

A content line contains a property name, optional parameters, a colon, and a value. Property and parameter names are case-insensitive; uppercase names are recommended when generating cards.

Long lines SHOULD be folded at 75 octets by inserting CRLF and one space or tab. A reader unfolds the line by removing that break and the following whitespace. Commas, certain semicolons, backslashes, and line breaks have specific escaping rules in values.
sections.plainLanguage:
A vCard is a set of labelled lines. It must start and end with the required markers, use UTF-8, and include a formatted name.

If a line is too long, it can continue on the next line after a space or tab. A reader removes that break when it reads the card.

sections.title: Values and Property Parameters
sections.content:
Each property has a value type. The standard types include text, URI, date, time, date-time, boolean, integer, float, UTC offset, and language tag. Date and time values use the basic format of ISO 8601. A URI value points to information rather than storing that information directly in the card.

Parameters add information about a property or its value. For example, LANGUAGE labels a language, VALUE identifies a value type, and PREF ranks a property instance from 1 to 100, with 1 most preferred. ALTID marks property instances as alternate forms of the same logical property.

Applications MUST ignore unrecognized private or registered parameter values. The RFC also defines parameters for property type, media type, sorting, geographic information, and time zones.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line has a value of a defined kind, such as text, a date, or a web address. Optional parameters add details, such as the language or which phone number is preferred.

sections.title: Information a vCard Can Contain
sections.content:
The properties cover general information, identity, addresses, communication, location, organizations, notes, security, and calendar links. Examples include FN for the formatted name, N for structured name parts, ADR for a delivery address, and TEL and EMAIL for contact methods.

The KIND property says whether a card represents an individual, group, organization, or location. If KIND is absent, an individual is assumed. An organization card MUST NOT contain MEMBER properties.

Most properties are optional, but every card must have FN. The format also permits extension properties and parameters, including private names that begin with X-.
sections.plainLanguage:
A card can hold a name, contact details, address, photo, organization, or other information. Its kind can say whether it describes an individual, group, organization, or place.

The formatted name is required. Other details depend on what the card needs to record.

sections.title: Matching Cards During Synchronization
sections.content:
vCard includes identifiers that help a synchronization program merge copies of the same contact. Equivalent UID values identify vCard instances that MUST be matched.

The PID parameter helps match individual properties. A CLIENTPIDMAP property maps a local source number to a URI, giving the property identifier global context. Properties with different names MUST NOT be matched. Other possible matches are left to the synchronization program.

The RFC's example shows two devices adding contact details. It uses identifiers to recognize matching values, while permitting a synchronization program to decide whether otherwise unmatched properties should be combined.
sections.plainLanguage: When two devices hold copies of a contact, identifiers help them recognize which cards and details refer to the same information. The format sets some required matching rules and leaves other decisions to the program that performs the merge.

sections.title: Privacy and Protecting Contact Data
sections.content:
vCards do not provide authentication or confidentiality by themselves. They can contain sensitive details, and email transport can expose them to monitoring, replay, or forgery. When confidentiality or authenticity matters, the RFC recommends sending vCards through a security mechanism such as S/MIME or OpenPGP.

A vCard can carry a public key in its KEY property. The RFC also recommends a SOURCE property when the originator cares about the freshness of the information; REV can indicate when the card was last updated.

Many properties can carry URIs, so the URI security considerations also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A vCard does not hide or authenticate its contents. If the details need protection, send the card using a security method that provides it.

sections.title: The vCard Media Type and Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC registers the text/vcard media type and lists .vcf and .vcard as file extensions. UTF-8 is the only permitted character set. Older media types including text/directory and text/x-vcard are marked deprecated in favor of text/vcard.

The RFC establishes registries for vCard properties, parameters, value data types, and values. A designated expert reviews new elements, which must be published in an RFC. Some changes require a Standards Track RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: vCard has an official media type and registries for its properties and values. New elements go through expert review and publication in an RFC.

viz.caption: A vCARD EXAMPLE SHOWN IN RFC 6350

data.title: Card for a person
data.code:
BEGIN:VCARD
VERSION:4.0
KIND:individual
FN:Jane Doe
ORG:ABC\, Inc.;North American Division;Marketing
END:VCARD

items.label: Person or entity
items.desc: The default when KIND is absent.

items.label: Group
items.desc: Can identify members with MEMBER properties.
